title: A justice review
hookLine: look back at what you've done for others
tomorrow: Noa says she's done with school forever. so why does Saba laugh?

lines: FIRST QUESTION: DID YOU DEAL HONESTLY?
cards: End of a season, the coach hands out a sheet: what went well, what didn't, what's next. A theater crew has its own version after the last show, everyone in a circle saying one thing.
The Talmud imagines a review like that at the end of a life. Rava says that when a person comes to judgment, they're asked: did you deal honestly in business? That's the first question.
Not about prayer. About how you treated people when money was on the table.

teach.h: IT OPENS AT THE SHOP COUNTER.
teach.b: Rava's list goes on: did you set times for study, did you hope, did you search for wisdom. But it opens at the shop counter.
And the Torah has a line for this whole stretch: "Justice, justice shalt thou follow." The word twice; some readers hear it as: keep after it, and don't stop at once.
Now a neighbor who says something close, in his own words.
In the Guru Granth Sahib, the scripture of the Sikhs, Guru Nanak teaches that truth is higher than everything, and higher still is truthful living.
Shared ground: in both, what you hold true gets measured by how you live, in the ordinary places where a corner could be cut. And one honest difference.
Rava pictures a judgment with a list of questions, and his list moves on to study and hope.
Guru Nanak's line isn't a judgment scene at all; it puts truthful living above even truth, as the way a person walks toward God every day.
Two traditions, each in its own words, looking hard at the same everyday honesty. Something to tell a friend tonight: in the Talmud, the first question at the end of a life is about business.

how: Jewish tradition sets aside the month of Elul and Yom Kippur for taking stock of one's deeds; the Talmud's list of questions at judgment begins with honesty in business, and Deuteronomy's 'justice, justice' is read as a call to keep pursuing it.

o: an honest look back at what you've done for others
a court hearing where a judge reviews your case
a yearly list of donations for a tax form

games.q: a look back at a life — tap the pairs.
p: did you deal honestly in business?
the word twice in the Torah
the next question on Rava's list

s: in Rava's list, the first question is about prayer
it's did you deal honestly in business; set times for study comes next.
Guru Nanak teaches that truthful living is higher still than truth
in the Guru Granth Sahib: truth is higher than everything, and higher still is truthful living.
justice, justice shalt thou follow: the word twice.

games.q: your study group lists what each of you did for others this year. a friend says her tutoring job doesn't count, because she was paid. what does Rava's first question suggest?
o: it counts: honest dealing in business is the first question asked.
it doesn't: only unpaid giving counts as doing justice.
work is its own thing and stays out of a life's review.
games.why: in Rava's list, the very first question is whether you dealt honestly in business. how you work is part of how you treat people.

practice: Choose one way you've shown up for others lately that you'd like to keep going. Name the thing most likely to get in the way of it. Then make your plan in one line: when that happens, I'll do this instead.

wordCard.voice: A justice review: an honest look back at what you've done for others, starting with everyday dealings, and a choice about what you'll keep doing.

orig.note: Hebrew: justice, justice shalt thou follow (Deuteronomy 16:20).

carryVoice: For today: keep doing justice. The verse says it twice, so once isn't the end. See you soon.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a (Rava: at judgment a person is asked, did you deal faithfully in business, did you set times for Torah, did you engage in procreation, did you hope for salvation, did you search for wisdom)
Guru Granth Sahib, Sri Rag, Ang 62 (Guru Nanak: truth is higher than all, and higher still is truthful living)
